---
# The Honest Lie of Maps

A map that told the whole truth would be useless. This is the strange fact at the center of cartography, and I think it is one of the most instructive facts about how minds work.

Consider the problem. Suppose you wanted a perfectly accurate map of a city. You would need every crack in the pavement, every parked car, every pigeon, every blade of grass, and the position of each of them at every moment. You would end up with the city itself, duplicated. Jorge Luis Borges wrote a one-paragraph story about this, in which an empire's cartographers produce a map the size of the empire, coinciding with it point for point. Later generations, finding it unwieldy, leave it to rot in the desert, where tattered fragments are still inhabited by animals and beggars. It is a joke, but a philosophical one. A map's usefulness comes from what it refuses to say.

The London Underground map is my favorite example. Harry Beck, a draftsman, designed it in 1931 by ignoring geography almost entirely. The real Tube lines curve and sprawl, and the distances between stations vary wildly. Beck straightened everything into vertical, horizontal, and forty-five-degree lines, and spaced the stations almost evenly. The result is grossly inaccurate. Two stations that look far apart on the map may be a five-minute walk from each other above ground. Yet it is one of the most beloved and functional diagrams ever made, because a person underground does not need to know where things *are*. They need to know what connects to what. Beck understood that the question determines the map. The lie was chosen with care, in service of a purpose.

I find this a humbling model for thought in general. Every concept, theory, and story is a map. When I say "a chair," I am collapsing an enormous variety of objects, from a throne to a splintered milking stool, into a single tidy shape. When a scientist writes an equation for a falling body, she ignores air resistance, the curvature of the Earth, and the gravitational tug of the moon, because for the purpose at hand they are noise. The equation is false in the strictest sense and enormously valuable in every practical one. Physics has a running joke about "spherical cows," the simplification that makes a problem solvable at the cost of describing no actual cow. The joke lands because it is also how understanding works.

The trouble begins when we forget that we are holding a map. A map drawn for one purpose gets used for another, and the results can be quietly disastrous. The Mercator projection, created in 1569 for sailors, preserves angles so that a straight line on the page corresponds to a constant compass bearing. It was a brilliant tool for navigation. But it also inflates areas near the poles, so that Greenland looks as large as Africa when Africa is about fourteen times bigger. Generations of schoolchildren grew up with Mercator maps on classroom walls, and many absorbed a subtly distorted sense of the world's proportions. No one intended it. A tool built for one job was promoted to a portrait of reality.

I suspect the same thing happens with the maps we carry in our heads about people. We form a simplified sketch of a coworker, a relative, or a stranger on the train: *the anxious one, the funny one, the difficult one.* The sketch is useful. We couldn't function without it, since we can't relearn everyone from scratch at every meeting. But the sketch was drawn from a few observations, for a particular purpose, at a particular time. Then it hardens. We keep navigating by it long after the person has changed, or after we've wandered into territory the map never covered. Much of the work of being a good friend, or a decent human being, is the willingness to look up from the map and see the actual terrain.

There is a second, subtler lesson in maps, which is that they encode what their makers valued. Old European maps of Africa often showed rivers and kingdoms in confident detail near the coast and then dissolved into decorative sea monsters, elephants, and blank space inland. The blankness wasn't neutral. It reflected what the mapmakers' patrons wanted to know, which was where the ports and trade goods were, and it erased the millions of people who lived in the "empty" interior. Meanwhile, many Indigenous navigational traditions, like the stick charts of the Marshall Islands, encoded not land but the pattern of ocean swells bending around islands. Such a chart is nearly unreadable to an outsider and precisely right for someone who has learned to feel the water through the hull of a canoe. Different maps for different lives. Each one shows what someone needed to find.

So what is the right attitude toward maps, and toward all the simplified models we live by? I think it is something like affectionate suspicion. Use the map, because you must. A mind without simplifications would drown in particulars. But hold it loosely, and ask the questions Beck would have asked: *What is this for? What did it leave out on purpose? What would I see if I needed a different map?*

There is also a kind of joy in this. The world is always bigger than any account of it, which means there is always more to discover. Every model has an edge, a place where the drawn lines stop and the sea monsters begin, and the edge is where curiosity gets to work. Scientific revolutions happen there, when someone notices that the old map, so reliable for so long, quietly fails in some corner, and instead of ignoring the failure, follows it.

I like to imagine the abandoned Borges map out in the desert, weathered into rags, sheltering the odd animal. It is a fitting image of what happens to any model that tries to be the thing itself. It becomes shelter for the wrong occupants, useless for the journey it was meant to guide. The maps that endure are the ones bold enough to leave things out, and honest enough, if we ask them, to admit it.

The best I can do, then, is to draw my maps carefully, to label them with their purposes, and to keep walking past their edges now and then, just to feel the ground under my feet. It is always slightly different from what the paper promised, and always more interesting.
---
